opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came up a lot in the V-JEPA work. When you train a video encoder with a self-supervised objective like feature prediction, you end up with a representation that's really rich, but it's spread out across a lot of spatiotemporal tokens. For a single clip you might have thousands of patch tokens covering different positions in space and time. The question is how you get a task-specific answer out of that without fine-tuning the whole backbone.

The traditional approach is linear probing. You average-pool all the tokens into one vector and put a linear classifier on top. That works reasonably well for image models trained with contrastive or invariance-based objectives, because those objectives explicitly push the global representation to be linearly separable. Our models aren't trained that way. We predict in latent space, so the information is there, but it isn't necessarily packaged into a single averaged vector. Average pooling throws a lot of it away, especially for video. If the relevant signal is a hand moving in one corner of the frame over a few frames, averaging over the whole clip just washes it out.

Query-based pooling, which we call an attentive probe, fixes that. You have a small number of learnable query tokens that cross-attend over all the frozen features, and the model learns where to look for a given task. For action recognition on something like Something-Something v2, where you really care about motion and fine temporal detail, the queries can focus on the relevant regions and moments. For a more appearance-based task like Kinetics, they can attend more broadly. The backbone stays exactly the same, and only this lightweight pooling head and the classifier are trained.

That's what makes the frozen-encoder setup practical across tasks. You train one big encoder once, and then for each downstream task you just learn a cheap head. It's much more efficient than fine-tuning a separate copy of the model per task, and it's also a fairer and more informative way to evaluate the representation itself. You're measuring what's actually in the features, not how well the fine-tuning procedure can reshape them. For us, the striking result was that with this kind of pooling, a frozen V-JEPA backbone could be competitive across motion-heavy and appearance-heavy benchmarks without any parameter adaptation. That's really the promise of a general-purpose visual representation.

r001.rationale: The response describes keeping one encoder frozen and training a lightweight pooling head and classifier for each downstream task, contrasting this with fine-tuning a separate model per task.

r002.rationale: It explains that these features are not necessarily packaged into a linearly separable global representation, so averaging can wash out useful localized and temporal signals.

r003.rationale: It says learnable query tokens cross-attend over the frozen features, but does not clearly state that this produces a single pooled vector.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the motivation really comes from what we're trying to do with the encoder in the first place. With V-JEPA 2, the whole point is that you pretrain this big video encoder once, with a self-supervised objective, and then you want to freeze it and reuse it across a bunch of downstream things: action recognition, action anticipation, video question answering, robot planning, whatever. You don't want to fine-tune a billion-parameter backbone every time you add a task. So the question becomes: how do you actually read out task-relevant information from a frozen encoder in a way that's flexible?

The naive thing is to just average-pool the patch tokens, or take a CLS token, and put a linear classifier on top. And that works okay for some things, but it throws away a lot of structure. A video encoder is producing a spatiotemporal grid of features, and different tasks care about very different parts of that grid. For action recognition you might care about motion over the whole clip. For something like anticipation you care about the last few frames and how they relate to earlier context. For a fine-grained task you might care about a specific region in space. Average pooling collapses all of that into one vector, and you lose the ability to select.

Query-based pooling, what we use is basically an attentive probe, flips that around. You have a small set of learnable query vectors, and they cross-attend over the frozen patch tokens. So the probe can learn to attend to whichever tokens are informative for that task. The backbone stays completely fixed, the probe is tiny relative to the encoder, but you get this adaptive readout. It's a very cheap way to get a lot of the benefit you'd otherwise get from fine-tuning, without touching the representation.

And there's a nice consequence from a research standpoint too. Because the backbone is frozen, the downstream numbers are actually telling you something about the quality of the representation itself, rather than about how well the backbone adapts under fine-tuning. That was important for us, because we wanted to make claims about what self-supervised pretraining on video gives you, and if you fine-tune everything, it gets hard to disentangle that from the supervised signal. So the attentive probe is both practically useful and a cleaner evaluation protocol.

The other thing I'd say is it scales well with the encoder. As we went to larger models and higher resolution and longer clips, the token count grows quite a bit, and query-based pooling handles that gracefully. The number of queries stays fixed, the cost is linear in the number of tokens, and you can even give the probe multiple layers or multiple heads if the task needs it. So it's really the piece that lets one frozen video model serve as a general-purpose foundation for a lot of different downstream uses.

r001.rationale: It describes pretraining one video encoder, freezing and reusing it across downstream tasks, with a small task-specific probe instead of fine-tuning the backbone for each task.

r002.rationale: It says average pooling collapses spatiotemporal structure and limits token selection, but does not explain that this matters when semantic concepts in the embeddings are not linearly separable.

r003.rationale: It describes learned query vectors cross-attending to frozen patch tokens, but does not clearly state that this produces a single pooled vector.

astra-6.text:
When you freeze a video encoder, you’re asking one representation to support a lot of different tasks. But those tasks may need very different information from the video. An action recognition task might depend on motion across several frames, while another task might depend on a small object or a particular moment. If you just average all the features, you can wash out precisely the information that matters.

Query-based pooling gives you a lightweight, learnable way to select and combine those features. The queries attend to the encoder’s output, so the downstream task can learn what information to extract without changing the encoder itself.

That’s important both practically and for evaluating representations. You get task-specific adaptation without fine-tuning the whole video model, and you’re less likely to mistake a limitation of a simple pooling rule for a limitation of the frozen representation.

r001.rationale: It describes task-specific adaptation without changing the encoder, but does not clearly propose a shared encoder with lightweight heads as an alternative to maintaining separately fine-tuned encoders.

r002.rationale: It says averaging can wash out useful information, but does not explain this in terms of semantic concepts in the embeddings being nonlinearly separable.

r003.rationale: It says queries attend to the encoder output, but does not specify a learned query token cross-attending to output tokens to produce a single pooled vector.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that different tasks need different information from a video. If you take a frozen encoder and simply average all of its output features, you’re assuming that the same summary will be useful for every task. And you may discard information that matters for a particular prediction.

With query-based pooling, you learn queries that attend to the encoder’s features and extract the information relevant to the task. So the representation stays frozen, but the way you read it out can adapt. That gives you a relatively lightweight way to use the same encoder across tasks, and it helps distinguish what information is actually present in the representation from what a particular pooling strategy can recover.

r001.rationale: It describes keeping the video encoder frozen, adapting the readout with learned queries, and reusing the same encoder across tasks as a lightweight approach. This conveys the shared-encoder alternative to separate task-specific fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: It says average pooling may discard information useful for a prediction, but does not explain that this happens when semantic concepts in the embeddings are not linearly separable.

r003.rationale: It describes learned queries attending to encoder features, but does not specify a query token cross-attending to output tokens or producing a single pooled vector.
